blogs.title: When Choking Isn’t GI: Neurogenic Dysphagia as a Clue to Chiari I
blogs.description: This post would examine the diagnostic approach to recurrent choking with both solids and liquids when laryngoscopy and endoscopy are normal. It would focus on how equal difficulty across consistencies points away from mechanical obstruction and toward bulbar or brainstem dysfunction, using Chiari I malformation as a reminder that persistent ‘ENT/GI-negative’ dysphagia deserves a neurological workup.

blogs.title: The Patient Who Desaturated Without Distress: Structural Causes of Acquired Central Hypoventilation
blogs.description: This post would explore the physiology behind preserved voluntary breathing with impaired automatic breathing, and how Chiari I can mimic acquired Ondine’s curse through brainstem compression. It would discuss the clinical red flags for central hypoventilation, why severe hypoxemia may occur without dyspnea, and when unexplained nocturnal or episodic desaturation should trigger a search for central neurologic pathology rather than primary pulmonary disease.

blogs.title: Mild AHI, Serious Problem: Reading Sleep Studies in Suspected Central Breathing Disorders
blogs.description: This post would use the case to highlight the limitations of type III sleep studies in suspected central sleep-disordered breathing. It would cover how lack of EEG can underestimate severity by using total recording time rather than true sleep time, why a low AHI can be falsely reassuring, and when formal polysomnography with EEG and capnography is needed to better characterize central apnea or hypoventilation.

blogs.title: The Missed Foramen Magnum: Why Old Imaging Deserves a Second Look
blogs.description: This post would focus on cognitive and systems-level diagnostic lessons from a 14-year delay caused in part by an overlooked crowded foramen magnum on prior CT. It would discuss when clinicians should personally revisit old imaging reports, which subtle CT features can hint at Chiari I before MRI is obtained, and how re-reviewing historical studies can unify years of seemingly unrelated symptoms.

blogs.title: Chiari I Is Common on MRI—But Who Actually Has Chiari Syndrome?
blogs.description: This post would tackle the modern tension between incidental tonsillar ectopia and clinically meaningful Chiari disease. It would review why millimeters of tonsillar descent alone do not define severity, how symptom-based reasoning should guide management, and how to think through conservative monitoring versus posterior fossa decompression in patients with brainstem, bulbar, or respiratory manifestations.

blogs.title: Occipital Headache, Scalp Allodynia, and the Haircut Clue: Atypical Pain Phenotypes in Chiari
blogs.description: This post would explore the less familiar pain presentations associated with Chiari I, including occipital headache, vertex pain, and scalp allodynia. It would discuss how these symptoms can be mislabeled as primary headache disorders such as nummular headache, whether occipital neuralgia or ‘burning vertex syndrome’ may overlap with Chiari, and why unusual cutaneous pain syndromes should prompt a broader neurologic differential when paired with other brainstem symptoms.
